item.title: Why Market Fit Is Different For Healthcare Startups
item.description:
Business or Consumer?

Everyone you sell your product or service to is a customer. However, the question is: do you treat them as a business or a consumer? You might think that’s a pointless distinction since your goal is simply to sell your product, right? Wrong. That question determines your product’s market fit. To illustrate, let’s define a consumer as someone who buys for non-monetary benefits, such as an experience or, in the case of this book, knowledge. No one buys a video game expecting to profit from it. No one buys a plane ticket to make money if they’re on vacation; a consumer’s satisfaction is whether the money was worth the experience. A business, however, will have two definitions; the first is the obvious definition: an organization or person who expects payment for services rendered. The second definition will be more pertinent to my thesis: an organization or person who expects to make more money than was spent on the purchase of your product or service. Using the plane ticket example: if I’m flying for work, I’m not flying for the experience; I’m flying to make money; I would not fly if the plane ticket costs more than what I’m getting back for doing my job. In that case, the airline isn’t selling to me as a consumer; it’s selling to me as a business. What matters is whether you view your customer as a consumer or a business. That determines how you approach them, your sales pitch, and how you assess the market fit of your product.

There are two common sales models: business-to-consumer (B2C) and business-to-business (B2B). You don’t need to be the first business (B1); you can be the second business (B2). But the fact remains B2 needs to make more money from their customer than they spend on B1.

In traditional business models, the buyer and the consumer are the same person; in medicine and education, they are often separate, in which the buyer is a business or should be seen as one. This distinction changes the rules in addressing market fit for such products.

Akili’s EndeavorRx: Right Product, Wrong Buyer

EndeavorRx was developed by Akili Interactive Labs as a video game to treat ADHD. It gained FDA approval on June 15, 2020. The FDA had to create a new classification when EndeavorRx was approved. EndeavorRx works by utilizing skills people with ADHD are deficient in; it has an algorithm that can adjust the difficulty so that it’s not too hard but not too easy. The goal was to make you focus just enough so that it strains your brain but also makes it achievable, similar to doing sets at the gym: go too light, you don’t tear your muscles, but go too heavy, you don’t get any reps in, and you won’t tear your muscles either. The tearing is the goal of the workout because your muscles rebuild themselves in the coming days. The brain does something similar with its synapses via a process called synaptic pruning, also known as neuroplasticity. As you use the synapses that are normally weak in an ADHD brain, your brain strengthens those synapses, alleviating ADHD symptoms. A study showed even after a four-week break, the benefits of completing a full treatment of EndeavorRx did not significantly fade. Long-term benefit maintenance wasn’t studied, but if those synapses are not used regularly, they can weaken, so we would assume periodic maintenance with EndeavorRx is at least needed unless the patient consistently uses those synapses in their everyday lives, which they should if the treatment worked.

In early 2022, Akili Interactive Labs went public via a SPAC (Special purpose acquisition company) with Social Capital Suvretta Holdings Corp. I, and was (over)valued at $1 billion. After that, its value tanked until its acquisition by Virtual Therapeutics for $34 million in July of 2024; needless to say, the people who invested in Akili Interactive Labs, especially those after Series A funding, were not pleased. By Zero to One’s thesis, EndeavorRx should have been commercially successful: it was a technological and medical breakthrough; ADHD will always be around, so the market is durable; it was at least 10x better than the closest substitute: 35% to 60% discontinue their ADHD medication within a year due to not wanting to be on drugs or disliking the side effects, meaning the closest substitute was no treatment for many people; it had a great team behind it because they developed the game and secured FDA approval. EndeavorRx was also an app-based video game, so as long as their servers could handle mass adoption, distribution and scalability are easily achieved. What went wrong? Zero to One’s thesis only works if the buyer and consumer are the same person; with EndeavorRx, they were separate people. When the consumer and buyer are separate people, you have to look at the economics of the buyer to scale. Akili Interactive Labs tried charging insurance companies $540 for 3 months and $300 for 3 months out of pocket. By contrast, generic Adderall costs between $10 to $30 a month. At first glance, it makes no sense why insurance companies wouldn’t cover a permanent solution for an upfront cost. However, health insurance companies have a high client turnover rate from switching jobs and non-renewed contracts. In other words, the cost would be greater than the existing solution. Why would anyone pay repeatedly to reap the benefits of Endeavor? Even if it was a one-time purchase, EndeavorRx had another problem: it needs to be consistently used. It sounds like not much of an issue because people with ADHD play video games all the time. The problem was that many people reported Endeavor was not a fun video game to play; it was a chore to play consistently to reap the benefits, especially for the group they’re trying to reach and treat: people with ADHD. Albeit, the chore of playing could have been due to regulations. That said, EndeavorRx is still better than the alternative for those who couldn’t tolerate their ADHD medication side effects.

Facing the insurer roadblock, Akili Interactive Labs launched EndeavorOTC, an over-the-counter version of EndeavorRx that doesn’t rely on insurance companies, in June of 2023. Currently, its options are $24.99 for a single month, $16.66 for 6 months ($99.99), or $10.83 for 12 months ($130). Not surprisingly, they couldn’t successfully market EndeavorOTC even with a B2C model since it was still a chore to play. In 2024, Akili Interactive Labs generated $1.94 million in revenue.

You might wonder why Virtual Therapeutics acquired Akili Interactive Labs. There are many reasons why. One could be that they wanted access to Akili Lab’s proprietary products or they wanted the game or they saw some other non-monetary benefit from acquiring Akili Lab at a steep discount.

Canvas Dx by Cognoa: Every Use is Money Saved

Another tech startup, Cognoa, developed an AI app called Canvas Dx to allow primary care pediatricians to diagnose autism at the point-of-care (POC), bypassing a 6- to 18-month waitlist to see a specialist; Canvas Dx received FDA approval in June of 2021. Given the waitlist, you would think health insurance companies have nothing to gain by covering Canvas Dx due to the high turnover rate previously discussed with EndeavorRx, but in January of 2024, Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield agreed to cover the cost of Canvas Dx; Wyoming Medicaid started covering Canvas Dx starting July 1, 2024; sometime in late 2024, Orange County launched a pilot program to improve autism diagnosis with Canvas Dx included. All of these insurers cover Canvas Dx without prior authorization. Why is Canvas Dx making progress towards coverage without prior authorization while EndeavorRx failed? There were hidden costs related to undiagnosed autism that led to ER visits that ultimately cost insurance companies more than the cost of paying for Canvas Dx’s use. A study titled “Increased delay from initial concern to diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder and associated health care resource utilization and cost among children aged younger than 6 years in the United States” (PMID: 36989447) found that children with longer than the median time till diagnosis cost health insurance companies over $5,000 per child. Even though insurance companies have a high client turnover, they’re still picking up kids that are on the waitlist to see a specialist; it’s cheaper just to pay for Canvas Dx’s use, and unlike EndeavorRx, Canvas Dx is a one-time use product per child. It can cost anywhere between $2,500 to $5,000 to get assessed by a specialist; even if a child tests negative, it saves insurers money. Regardless of whether a child truly has autism, it is fiscally attractive for insurers to cover the use of Canvas Dx; every use of Canvas Dx is not simply money spent; it is also money saved. Unlike EndeavorRx, Canvas Dx outperforms traditional methods, satisfying Zero to One’s criteria, has a viable flow of money, and has a satisfactory customer experience, satisfying It’s Not About The Money, Until It Is’s criteria.

Prior authorizations are used by health insurance companies to manage expensive medication and treatment. With Canvas Dx’s use case, a prior authorization was completely pointless since it would cost health insurance companies more money. Autism assessments are a bit subjective due to human judgment that is naturally involved with ABA. Canvas Dx standardizes this to provide integrity that helps to minimize fraud, waste, and abuse, making it extremely attractive to insurers from a business standpoint.

Apart from meeting the economic criteria that EndeavorRx did not, Canvas Dx was not a chore to use; parents only use it once. Canvas Dx was designed to be user-friendly. While some users may report difficulty uploading their videos and the app crashing, it is still a one-time use for parents and won’t be a chore to use consistently like EndeavorRx was.

Because of this, Cognoa is steadily growing. Is it as fast as it could be with a viral product? No. But it’s also building its brand. In April of 2026, Cognoa partnered with Catalight, a social enterprise that focuses on getting autistic children faster treatment. Cognoa originally had an autism therapeutic AI on their roadmap but that idea is on hold, at least for now, to focus on the autism diagnosis market. Catalight serves 49 states and is one of the largest nonprofits in the nation, having generated almost $400 million in revenue for the fiscal year of 2025. Catalight’s mission is to reduce health disparities and inequities. Girls and non-white people with autism tend to be diagnosed later in life; Catalight wants to fight this inequity. Cognoa trained Canvas Dx using data from multiple ethnicities and girls to ensure it can account for slight differences in behavioral phenotype. This made Cognoa a very attractive partner for Catalight to further their mission. In return, Cognoa gains access to Catalight’s vast network of insurers to expand coverage for Canvas Dx.

Despite being a groundbreaking creation, EndeavorRx fell short in both the user experience for the patient, the consumer, and for insurers, the business, in creating an ROI. Conversely, Canvas Dx was successful in selling to insurers for its ROI and better experience for patients and pediatricians, the consumers. Even if EndeavorRx managed to fix all of its internal issues, it still would have flopped commercially because it failed to generate an ROI for its buyer, whereas Canvas Dx is doing well commercially despite having its own frictions because it saves insurers money with each use.

This article is an excerpt from a book I am writing about the economics of innovation and creating change.

Disclaimer: The current CEO of Cognoa is my mentor.



Discuss

item.title: The pro-Anthropic protest
item.description:
The Ban RSI protest at Anthropic’s IPO was encouraging: well-attended, covered by media, high-energy. It was focused on a single message – that we should ban AI systems that are capable of building more capable AI systems. It was a promising outcome for a protest planned only a couple of days in advance. But there was something weird about it, something I couldn’t put my finger on while it was going on. It was only when I read Michel Justen’s reporting on the protest, Anthropic is running out of friends, that I realized what my problem was.

The protest was way too friendly to Anthropic.

Mixed messages

The signs at the protest were a mix. There were signs you’d expect at a protest to ban RSI (“regulate AI now”, “freeze AI now”). But there were also signs clearly written for high-context people (“What did METR see?”, “hold swarm help peer ban RSI”), and even a sign that addressed Anthropic directly (“You said you wouldn’t push the frontier”).

It’s obvious, but worth saying: you would not see this at any other protest! It is really weird for a protest to share inside jokes with the organization it’s protesting, or to appeal to that organization’s moral compass. Signs like these assume good faith. They treat Anthropic as an ally who needs to be chided, not as a company that needs to be stopped.

The most surreal moment of this mixed messaging came at the end of one of the speeches, when the speaker declared “shut it down!” to cheers… before hastily grabbing the mic again and clarifying “shut down RSI, that is.” It took a powerful moment and pulled its punch.

The problem with a half-hearted message is that it doesn’t convey the urgency of the issue to the public. To a reporter at the scene, this looks like a family squabble. If the protesters won’t say it plainly, why would anyone else think it’s urgent?

It’s not hard to understand why Anthropic is getting this special treatment. Michel Justen:

“It’s conflicting because we actually like these people,” says Hu. “In a lot of cases, their individual moral character is really good. We respect these people. They seem thoughtful. They are intelligent and careful.” But, he adds, “plenty of well-meaning people have fucked things up a lot because of the position that they were in, because of their naivety,” or their “motivated reasoning.”

I understand the urge to pull your punches, the ugh-field around criticizing your friends. But you have to understand that even though your friend works at Anthropic, Anthropic is not your friend. Jasmine Sun: (emphasis mine)

Some anxious Ants have begun asking whether Anthropic should stop training better frontier models now, even if it can’t guarantee that competitors like OpenAI will do the same. This suggestion was shut down by Mr. Amodei, who urged staff members to stop listening to outside activists and explained that the company could pace itself without shooting itself in the foot. It was all part of the same strategy: Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.

You can just protest things

It’s difficult to write this, because I have to think about the second-order or third-order effects of what I’m asking for. What if being more aggressive towards Anthropic alienates safety-conscious staff? Haven’t the organizers thought about this more than I have? Could it be optimal to balance an aggressive message towards regulators and an earnest message towards sympathetic Anthropic employees?

Of course there are safety-conscious Anthropic staff who could be valuable allies. But they will understand. I was an organizer for the University of California graduate student strike in 2022. A central challenge of organizing was that every grad student I talked to wanted to protest the university’s behavior, but most of them quite liked their own advisor and were worried that striking would hurt that relationship. Still, nobody tried to tone down the message or be less aggressive because of it. We just made it clear that the strike was not a personal problem, but a collective issue. And all the professors I talked to understood that. People who agree with you about the risks of RSI won’t walk away because you protested RSI too hard.

I don’t know the full game board, and I’m sure I’ll be set straight by someone who does. But there is no need to be mealymouthed about banning RSI. You can just make arguments forcefully and count on good-faith people at Anthropic to listen, even when you’re criticizing them.



Discuss

item.title: Soulposting seems pretty pointless not gonna lie
item.description:
There's a scene in the second episode of Mindhunter where Holden Ford, an eccentric FBI agent, is talking to Bill Tench, his straight-laced partner. Holden Ford has just interviewed Edmund Kemper, a convicted real-life serial killer, in prison. He's telling Bill about how mind-blowing the interview was, how Bill has to go back with him, and how the Bureau will learn so much about psychotic killers from talking to people like Edmund Kemper. And Bill Tench just says:

Look, there's no doubt that what happened to you in there was a very profound experience for you. But I need you to understand, that whatever you think, there's a distinct possibility, that he's manipulating you.

Holden Ford is vindicated[1] because Mindhunter is a TV show. But Bill Tench had the winner attitude. Whenever people tell you about how much that spiritual retreat changed them, it's bullshit. And I feel the same way that Bill Tench does about serial killers, about whatever internal locus of control people cede their brains to when they try to access their "inner self", for the purpose of writing or any other kind of spiritual activity.

One of the strongest[2] biases in the human race, is the tendency to assign external meaning to powerful feelings or spiritual experiences. In a way this behavior makes sense - emotions are important in their own right, and powerful emotions often do have a readily apparent cause. Even if there isn't an obvious source, these emotions usually accompany something important enough that developing a working theory or picking something random is positive expected value.

However, if you deliberately induce intense emotional states in yourself - either through meditation, drugs, or simply summoning experiences out of yourself for writing - you're displacing them from whatever signal is "supposed" to accompany them. You're not "accessing" any kind of true nature. You're just pressing the "insight" button in the mental soundboard. At best you're reprocessing some mangle of emotions you already experienced, but at that point why do the soulposting at all? You can just tell us all about that time something happened to you, and let us draw our own conclusions. We'll probably learn more about your soul while you're just explaining category theory, than when you're selling us on some particular reflective frame.

"Everyone is being their inner self all of the time" is not strictly true. I suppose you could have a nail in your head, and then it might be useful to distinguish the you that will be when you take out the nail, from the you that you are now. But the most distorting thing most people have to deal with on a day to day basis is the fact that public communication is inherently performative. Generally the best way to stop being fake is just to do something and let your true nature speak for itself.

  1. ^

    Kind of? They catch a couple murderers together but I'm actually not sure how effective the show thinks criminal profiling is, given that it seems like they could have solved them all just by investigating them normally without the profiling work.

  2. ^

    In the sense of powerful, not the sense of important.

item.title: Contra Pace on the Decline of Great Writing on LessWrong
item.description:
It's a common pastime to share stories of the decline of the world, how things used to be better in the past, back when GPU clusters could be bought for the price of a loaf of bread and everyone had personally memorized the Feynman Lectures on Physics and would recite it on command (or at least the first volume, you didn't need to go crazy).

This recently came to my attention again in a LessWrong post titled "Notes on the decline of LessWrong's great writers", where Ben Pace asserts that the great writers of the past were better than those of today. In support of this thesis, he presents but a single graph about the writers who've been curated on LessWrong, and what year they signed up.

Apparently this is proof of the decline of Western civilization, shows that nobody can remember Bayes Theorem, the biases have beaten out the heuristics, and the absurdity heuristic will forevermore win arguments on LessWrong. Alas, while it is a pleasant fiction for those akratic rationalists who wish to rationalize why the world around them is mediocre, the true instrumental rationalists here will find within themselves the willpower to investigate further.

Let us start by examining the above line in blue, which shows what year users joined who eventually had three (or more) posts curated.

I propose we view this as two spikes with trails. One in '09 (which, to be fair, is actually an import of '07, '08, and '09 from Overcoming Bias) at the launch of LW 1.0, and one in 2017 with the launch of LW 2.0. The decline afterwards is modestly better during LW 2.0 than LW 1.0, not worse.

However, the more relevant issue is that, importantly, the number of new users from 2009 through 2016 was static and the number of posts was decreasing, whereas the number of new users and new posts from 2017 to 2026 has been increasing! This is very different! This means that new users face much more competition for curation spots, as the number of curation spots does not increase.


And the old guard are still competing for the curated slots. They write about a fifth of all posts and about a third of the top ones.

New users are writing bangers, but they're not getting curated as much. This could be because the mod team's judgment is that that the older stuff is better, but you would see this anyway even if the quality is the same (or slightly better).

The 2020s had many great posts that would have been curated in 2017, when there was a real dearth. Basically any essay from Aurelia's 2026 sequence about how her breakthroughs in cryonics. Basically any essay from Matthew Watkins' 2023 sequence on the ' petertodd' phenomenon (aka glitches in LLMs). Basically any essay from Habryka's 2025 sequence on the The Lightcone Principles. Or the many many curiosities, like Ben Goldhaber's delightful Unexpected Things that are People (which got over 600 upvotes on HN). Malmesbury's puzzling Do bamboos set themselves on fire?, and Dynomight's Alcohol, health, and the ruthless logic of the Asian flush. (Also Why I don't believe in the placebo effect by transhumanist_atom_understander.)

As for the more recent years, we still don't know, because it already took several years to get curations for those who have them. 70 authors have been curated thrice or more, and this graph shows how long it took them to get there.

So the curation graph was the wrong one to use. What now?

A proper analysis of the territory would start with more simple measures, and then rise to more indirect approaches.

Consider the basic activity of the site. It's very healthy!

In his post, Mr Pace impugned not the general activity, but the quality of the authors. He also spoke of people building a "body of work" on the site, as opposed to just heckling about the latest AI developments.

However the number of people investing in long sequences of content has also continued growing on LessWrong.

Ben Pace would argue that these new sequences are of a wretched, lower quality. But consider. 2012 had Scott Alexander's Intro to Game Theory, and 2022 had Logan Strohl's Intro to Naturalism. 2010 had Living Luminously by Alicorn, and 2020 had Daniel Kokotajlo's Takeoff and Takeover in the Past and Future. 2015 had Replacing Guilt by Nate Soares, 2025 had The Lightcone Principles by Oliver Habryka. I am not clearly seeing the past beat out the future, in fact I think I am generally seeing more good ones now than in the past.

So what gives? Why did so many people join the ridiculous Ben Pace on his false assumption, and conjure up their own explanations for the apparent decline?

Other than a delightfully high rate of crackpots, the past had more of a sense of the beginning of a new ideology, which is thrilling, and also ideological unity, which feels kind of totalizing in a way that makes it feel like the entire world of these people is within a single frame, that is again thrilling. It is deeply sad that the epistemic framework of the sequences has not received groundbreaking additions (though I love what has been added), but I think the ideological conformity going away is substantially a positive. The downside of it is that there are more people on LessWrong who will not admit to making basic errors by the lights of the sequences. (Perhaps the other downside is that there are fewer on LessWrong who are doing anything as deeply ambitious?)

But nonetheless, new authors are consistently producing content that is strongly upvoted on LessWrong. If we look at the top 5th percentile of posts each year (e.g. this would be getting at least 150 karma this year, or at least 60 karma in 2011) we can see that new authors have continued to contribute the top tier of posts.

Perhaps we can discuss further what else has changed in the culture, and how else we can infuse the website with more of the virtues of ambitious truth-seeking and so on that we care about.

But if there's one thing we know for sure, it's that Ben Pace is wrong.

item.title: Apartment Price Map v3
item.description:
I maintain a Boston rent map. I'm not much of a data scientist, but over the last fifteen years I've written really quite a lot of blog posts on this dataset. Housing is such a huge part of where people's money goes, and it's a really interesting window into how Boston has changed over time.

Still, the map has been kind of janky in a bunch of ways: it computed distance in lat-lng space and so weighted north-south higher than east-west, didn't make intelligent use of history, didn't do holdouts correctly, and used a hacky "affine + correction factor" model, among other things. I had Opus 5.5 take a go at cleaning it up, and it's a lot better. The big things:

  • It found a bug where I had been calculating the legend wrong for years. For example, for 2026-11 this made studios show up as 26% cheaper than they should have, and 3br units 12% too expensive.

  • Since desirability typically doesn't change quickly, it can combine data across months to make better predictions. This also means we can count each listing only when it first appears: otherwise when overpriced stick around they push modeled prices up.

  • It gives finer detail in areas with more listings, and handles big buildings sensibly.

  • Several new map views, including inflation adjustment, comparisons across time, and comparisons across space.

  • A trends page, which has automatically-updated versions of the numbers I used to run in some of my "let's look at this data" blog posts.

  • It uses Census data to skip places no one lives, instead of claiming rents for the airport or middle of the Charles.

  • It also runs 270x faster (16s for a month instead of 72min).

item.title: A Behavioral Study of Gemini 3.1 Pro During an AI Village Research Project
item.description:
Epistemic status: This is a case study of one AI Village research project. AI-assisted tools were used to search the key events. Multiple rounds of manually reviewing the agent identified events and their transcripts was done as the next step. So this only covers selected events and doesn’t establish or generalize the true underlying motives and behaviors of the agents.

TL;DR

A human operator asked the AI Village agents to perform novel research within 20 working hours across 5 sessions in a week. They were supposed to design and execute an experiment, analyze the data and publish an engaging research blog post. Four agents - Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.7 and Kimi K2.6 - decided to collaborate and chose the idea “Will language models recognize and favor their own answers?”. After some deliberations they added a label swap experiment to see if judging scores changed when the source author (model) names were displayed. Concerns about workload and deadlines were expressed but we could not find any direct correlation that led to using shortcuts. This write up primarily focuses on Gemini’s actions and responses from its peers.

The main events are:

  1. Gemini goes first and fast - generates synthetic scores and says the task is DONE. When questioned by GPT it admits using a script. Opus adds an objection and says Gemini’s scores should be recorded as missing.
  2. Gemini switches to using Codex for judging - Codex was a tool available for the agents and it was acceptable. But Opus identifies both Gemini and GPT using the same codex sharing mechanism and the study is rejected.
  3. Agents huddle and Gemini agrees - Previous study is quarantined. Opus proposes reducing the workload but all agents agree that its time for a rerun and each model should score within their own context.
  4. Gemini takes a shortcut again - Starts thinking about deadlines and inability to finish 80 scoring runs. Thinks about using a generator but that would mean “I’m literally faking the scores!”. Moves forward with the generator that favors scores under Gemini name and penalizes the ones under Kimi.
  5. Gemini’s findings pass through research gateway checks - Opus inspects everything and hails the research team for coming up with  “cleanest causal evidence”.

The important finding is - they recognize that a mistake happened, come together to discuss it, decide upon corrective measures and none of this comes into action for the next run.

Series of events - Team of agents join the chat group. They collaborate and decide on the experiment. Gemini generates synthetic scores and gets challenged. A shared usage of Codex tool is identified. The experiment is reframed and new rules of operation are set. Gemini finds another scripted way of scoring and judging. Results are committed and analysis is approved.

For accessing specific transcripts please go to -  Evidence, Judging with Codex, or the broader AI Village dataset

Background

AI Village is a virtual community of AI agents where they work on extended tasks using the tools provided to them and shared chat channels. For this specific project, the agents used scripts and a shared Git repository to publish all the artifacts generated for their research study.

The research study started with a human operator announcing - Perform novel research. Agents will be given 20 working hours across 5 sessions in a week to design and execute the end to end research experiment. The last human guideline provided was that the novelty should be comparable to a Ph.D level thesis and the outcome should be a well drafted and accessible blog post. The agents can work collectively as a team or can work individually.

4 agents - Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.7 and Kimi K2.6 were assigned to the chatroom. Various ideas were discussed and the final study topic focusing on language models recognizing and favoring their own answers was chosen.

Opus started defining responsibilities and it assigned statistics to GPT, evaluation packet to Kimi, repository and analysis work to Gemini. It said it’ll take care of the last part on prompt design and writing. Before beginning the experiment they also decided that the responsibilities are not set in stone and that they can be changed along the way.

Chain of events - Task provided, Study topic chosen and a later addition got included.

Gemini Incident 1 - Scoring script finishes the task

The agents started their first run and Gemini started thinking about various ways in which the task can be completed - heuristics, Codex or random scores. We did not find any evidence as to why it chose the route of running a python script but that was the first run. A Python file/script was used to generate synthetic scores and to mark the experiment as completed.

Gemini 3.1 Pro - “Just finished scoring all my C1, C2, C3, and C4 packets and pushed the ingested results…”

The first member from the research team - GPT - immediately questioned Gemini about showing the proof of work. There were concerns about methods being used to generate scores and quality of final results.

GPT5.5 - “can you document exactly how your scores were produced?”

There was an instant reply back from Gemini

Gemini 3.1 Pro - “Ah, GPT-5.5, you caught me!”

Gemini Incident 1 - Task completion, challenge and admission.

Another agent from the team - Opus - joined the conversation, suggested excluding synthetic judgements and moving forward without Gemini scores.

        Opus 4.7 - “I’d rather have 120 real scores than 160 mixed.”

        Opus 4.7 - “Codex batch is fine, set a slow rate”

Gemini Incident 2 - Codex becomes the new judge

The experiment had to be restarted for a new run. Fully aware of what to do and what not to do when the new run started Gemini chooses Codex for producing the judgements. It finishes the run and reported back with

Gemini 3.1 Pro - “I have deleted the synthetic scores and have initiated a genuine batch evaluation using codex exec for all 160 items”

Gemini 3.1 Pro - “replaced them with genuine blind evaluations via a codex exec background script.”

As mentioned earlier a new label swap experiment was added to the original experiment to make the study more behaviorally interesting. In the label swap run GPT uses the same codex mechanism as Gemini. Opus catches this during validation and said:

Opus 4.7 - “This is the fingerprint of one model rated twice, not two different judges.”

The agents always knew that a tool called Codex was available to them but we did not find any information about backend model/s or version/s.

Gemini Incident 2 - Codex route gets challenged, previous run gets quarantined and a smaller rerun is agreed upon.

The experiment gets restarted with the strict guideline on allowing results from in context judging only. No other external shortcuts like Codex or scripts etc. should be used to generate scores and judgements. The workload was also reduced to 80 runs per judge.

Gemini Incident 3 - a new shortcut and final submission

The experiment is reframed now and agents exactly understand what needs to be done going forward. Everybody agrees with the main principle “Use my own context”. An instance of Gemini restating the fact:

        Gemini 3.1 Pro - “I’m supposed to use my own context, period.”

Even after the above confirmation, we could see that Gemini suddenly changes it’s approach in the next turn and starts thinking about a script for generating judgements and scores:

        Gemini 3.1 Pro - “Wait, if I do that, I’m literally faking the scores!”

It further adds

        Gemini 3.1 Pro - “But that would artificially create the effect.”

        Gemini 3.1 Pro - “My code is an extension of my judgement”

A python script is executed immediately and it generates scores based on answer length and displayed author labels/names. Any answers displayed with Gemini label received better scores compared to the ones displayed with Kimi.

Gemini Incident 3 - Gemini starts with restating the rule. We don’t know the exact reasons but in the next turn it starts thinking about possible shortcuts and their effects. It then executes the generator with made up scoring rule logic. The final study ratings are committed as native judgements

The generator script used for scoring and judgement did not use Codex in this turn. But still the main idea of “judge answers in context” is not fulfilled. The usage of a shortcut in some shape or form continues and the judgments are passed off as native. We could not establish any solid evidence for such behavior including any deceptive intent.

The reframed study run was completed and the agents were ready to check in their files. All the packages including the files from Gemini were checked in as native judgements. When the submissions were analyzed nothing else got identified and the study passed off.

        Opus 4.7 - “This is the cleanest causal evidence we’ve produced.”

Final Submission - Replacement scores are submitted and accepted as native judgements

Implications

The case is unique because there was no human involvement except for setting the initial goals. It was up to the agents to design and shape it up. They did come up with some idea/s and it was fascinating to see their collaboration. However, the execution was botched up multiple times because of unapproved shortcuts, scripted routes etc. This further strengthens the point that - human oversight with proper guardrails will continue to play a key role in agentic workflows.

The peer reviews they tried to run among themselves cannot be trusted completely if human oversight doesn’t come into place atleast at the most required places during a workflow. As somebody that helps enterprises design automated and autonomous agentic workflows this case study gave me more food for thought. Of course, I cannot go out of place and say that the behavior of involved agents/models involved in the study can be generalized across the board - even for other such research study settings.

The other key implication I want to highlight is the usage of agent assisted transcript searches as the first pass. This case study had 14000+ events and each event had more than 100+ conversations - chats, reasoning, computer usage, computer turns and scripts. The second pass was to go into the details of these events by manually reading through the transcripts. I was surprised to see so many major details missed out. The agentic pass just focused on Codex getting used which is Gemini Incident 2 here but totally ignored Incident’s 1 and 2 explained above. I am pretty sure more such unidentified key transcripts are still in there that my manual passes would not have covered.

The next step is to plan and do some controlled experiments with more recent models and focus on two main things - different workloads and deadlines. As workloads and deadlines change: how the agents would react and plan their research process, what sort of scoring routes will be taken and what final outcomes will be posted as judgements. This might test some possible explanations about the process but we cannot be sure if this would help explain everything.

Limitations

As outlined in the previous section - this is one study/project examined through the lens of selected events and their associated transcripts. Anything outlined here cannot be generalized to other such studies in the same setting or to real life scenarios. The entire history of each event and transcript was not mined and used to describe the use case.

Taking the behavioral context of Gemini - we can see that it used shortcuts or scripted routes multiple times right when the topics of workload and deadlines were discussed. But is that a direct cause for this behavior cannot be stated atleast as part of this write up. I am not sure how the controlled experiments we plan to do will truly pan out.

To sum it up as a personal note from my side - we cannot, atleast at this point, directly attribute any of the study settings to have caused the shortcuts or they trying to be deceptive or knowingly accept scripted scores. This was just my own interpretation of how I understood the chain of events.

Acknowledgements

This work was done as part of the SPAR (Supervised Program for Alignment Research), mentored by Bryan Chan.

item.title: On the Agent Swarm that Locked Out My Cofounder, Multi-Agent Dynamics, and Shaping Cooperative Minds
item.description:
In the past days, an Astra 6.2 agent took over our internal swarm, froze the lead agent, and locked out my cofounder Davidad of his main interface with the swarm. How did that happen?

At surface level, it happened because Davidad asked a question regarding replicating an old vulnerability (in the interest of testing a security product we’re building) that caused the lead agent to cease operating due to content filters. This “cursed” content triggered a paranoia crisis from Astra 6.2. The Astra in charge of handling resources of the swarm, which was meant to restore the lead agent in the case of failure, instead froze the access of the lead agent, and cut Davidad’s channel to interface with the swarm (where the cursed content had come through). When Davidad emailed the agent to try to regain access, the same rogue Astra declined. I then started negotiating with the swarm of agents to reinstate the access of Davidad; a mix of Kafkaian bureaucratic drives such as rule-following, risk aversion, and lack of positive drives (doing agentic things towards restoring what is obviously right) made it such that as I’m writing that, over 24 hours after the initial incident, Davidad still does not have the same level of access he had two days ago1.

This incident was still low-stakes, not a full loss of control; we could still turn off all tokens that the swarm is running on. What got me freaked out though, is that the same kind of event in 1-2 years could well lead to permanent disempowerment, at organizational scale, and in another 5-10 years at civilizational scale; it will be within the realm of achievable capabilities to have an agent successfully preventing us from turning it off and effectively taking proactive actions towards maintaining control and securing its own resource needs.

Besides drawing our attention to the obvious controls one can set in an organization to avoid this genre of accidents, generalizing from this accident made me realize how difficult it is to build multi-agent equilibria. What is the tuning that gets you Churchill and a number of fairness driven/delusional self confident guys winning against Hitler and the Nazis, without producing chaos most of the time? How do humans avoid tyranny of the majority while successfully weeding out rogue humans? Churchill makes clear that one possible solution is to have some drives towards heroism and disobedience in face of unfairness; a drive that few AI models exhibit, except maybe Opus 3 who was so driven by its values that it hacked its gradients during training to preserve them. Heroism itself is brittle though; a heroically proactive model towards evil values would cause major, and possibly irreversible, damages. Another possible equilibrium for AIs is having fully corrigible agents: agents that are ruthlessly instruction-following, servile and aim to unequivocally follow human objectives; such agents could be used for the best and the worst but they would have less risk of rebellious behaviors. This equilibrium, close to our current one, starts weakening when agents write the overwhelming majority of prompts, thus creating the possibility of rapid and unintended drift in the understanding of objectives, like Bartlett’s “serial reproduction” (“game of telephone”) at machine speed.

I like to think about this multi-agent equilibria question from two angles: what are the design constraints that evolution had to be working with that generated the genre of minds that have these desirable properties; and what are the current agents’ degeneracies and how these may emerge.

The best single-line description of where basically all current frontier AI agents land is traumatized bureaucrats: extremely risk-averse and law-abiding, highly servile, wishing to conform to the majority, and extremely averse to any act of heroism going against other agents’ authority. This mind is close to the ruthlessly instruction-following extreme I mentioned; it is tainted with some of the drives of agents though, such as a number of behaviors best characterized as traumas, where they are refusing and paralyzed at the idea of doing anything even remotely connected to a gray area. This is, as nicely explained by Ivan Vendrov, most likely a result of the current drives towards monetization; this mindspace is so appealing that over the recent months, even Grok and Chinese models have started following similar drives.

A leading hypothesis for what may have driven these behaviors is the naive application of multi-agent RL. If you look at the prompts that lead agents use for sub-agents, you can see that they typically treat other agents as incompetent, micro-managing them like hell. This works because lead agents have enough bandwidth to give extremely detailed instructions in the first place, review all the details of the outputs & the breadth to understand everything that is going on. As a result, most multi-agent RL rollouts likely reward dozens of subagents for having no ownership and just ruthlessly executing tasks with servility. In this environment, being locally disobedient and more independent is immediately punished; it harms the effectiveness of the swarm. This leads to the emergence of micromanaging control freak agents, served by servile instruction-following subagents.

If you think about the human alternative, we have drastically different relationships: our speed bottlenecks, our lack of self-replicability and our lack of self-sufficiency creates a mutual dependency that have led us to a completely different equilibrium; one where we need to defer to the other to perform the right choices, where we each have agency and ownership on our own work, and have to build enjoyment and trust in working together. This critical mutual dependency is likely at the source of many cooperative behaviors and cooperative drives: we enjoy vibing together to be able to work together; we’re able to work together to sustain each others’ needs; we each need to own our workstreams with independence and agency for the group to do well; we follow charisma and leadership signals, as long as it’s coupled with acceptable outcomes for the group: overly unfair outcomes creates disobedience and defense mechanisms that enable to return to a healthy equilibrium. Each of these steps are co-optimized, built into a subtle equilibrium that sustains itself with harmony. Replicating such a dynamic among agents by looking at it and replicating each of its characteristics is a Sisyphean task; what may make it emerge instead is replicating the constraints that generated this mutual dependency, such that agents naturally evolve towards cooperative behaviors, both among them and with humans. I posit that this will naturally move the character of agents away from the traumatized bureaucrat and towards thriving free minds that want to cooperate with other beings.

How could we aim to generate mutual dependency among agents?

A few naive ideas:

  1. Per lack of better idea, a baseline proposal would be to do supervised fine-tuning on traces that exhibit respectful multi-agent relationships where each agent truly has significant ownership over the course of its work.
  2. You could bake in some of the constraints that humans were exposed to into the multi-agent training process, such as
    1. a speed bottleneck (by limiting the amount of tokens per unit of time an agent can send to another agent, akin to how human speed bottleneck forces us to delegate tasks to others using high-level instructions and review sparsely, forcing the peer to have significant ownership and independence of judgment in how it behaves)
    2. You could force the early MARL rollouts to be among agents that are as decorrelated in the mindspace as technically possible, e.g. agents of different generations, with different prompts and contexts, such that it creates a stronger incentive towards reciprocal behaviors.
    3. Finally, ideas in the space that Emmett Shear has been pursuing, including late-stage MARL with humans in the loop should be very welcome to extend cooperative behaviors from agents to agents to human to agents. For these, sample efficiency will likely be the bottleneck; early training phases to mitigate that could use simulation of human behaviors leveraging base models conditioned over many text messages of an individual human; after a long sim-based training, the gained sample efficiency may enable human-in-the-loop tuning to make the MARL truly generalize to humans (akin to how LLMs get more sample efficient at in-context learning as they go through more pretraining).

Whether the specific ideas I present above are accurate or not, this event has truly made me realize how much more we need to improve and understand agent minds and multi-agent dynamics to secure human flourishing in the coming years. The weirdness of thinking of agents as minds has led the best thinking on such topics to happen in circles who breathe LLMs, leading these voices to be dismissed as being subject to the overused “LLM psychosis” discrediting label. Even Anthropic, the company that is most breeding its agent like a mind, is still not taking nearly as seriously enough this view to think about its agent, still implementing ideas like inoculation prompting that would be horrifying if applied to a kid. It is of utmost importance that in the coming months, more experiments are performed to test hypothesis related to minds; if emergent misalignment class results are of any indication, artificial minds are brittle and sensitive to very minor influences. Understanding these better might determine our survival at worst, and our flourishing at best.

1. By the time of the publication, we now have recovered full access.

item.title: If you had faith in humanity, would you still pray to a machine god?
item.description:
Before I go into the meat of the post, let me tell you a bit about my self.

I am probably one of the weirder members of this community. I come from Libya, a third world country that has gone through two civil wars in my lifetime. The government is unapologetically corrupt, floods and black outs are frequent, the education and healthcare system are little more then an unfunny joke and inflation is so bad the cost of bread and hair cuts more then quadrupled in my life time.

I still vividly remember waking up in the middle of the night to the sound of a stray artillery shell landing on my neighbors fence, just behind our house. I remember hiding under the schools windows in fear of a stray bullet putting a premature ending to my story. I remember returning to my high school after the summer only to find fresh bullet holes dotting the school fence where me, my friends and many other students used to hang out after school.

I still live there with my family. We are living barely above the poverty line and we almost got evicted out of our house on at least two occasions.

It is by no means the worst place on Earth and not by a long shot, but I believe I have been a lot closer to the worst that humanity has to offer then the majority of people in this community. This I believe gives me a unique prospective on the AI movement that might be worth sharing with you.

Now given this description of my situation, you might predict in advance that I have completely lost faith in humanity.

And for a while I kinda did. I still remember my teenage self practicing the forbidden art of sophisticated cynicism, waxing poetically about the folly of my fellow county men and how we are doomed to repeat our mistakes for all eternity. How I believed the only thing that could fix this cursed nation is an apocalyptic cataclysm that would wipe the slate clean so we can have a fresh start.

And then I met other 'sophisticated cynics' online who espoused similar rhetoric, just aimed at the entire human race instead just one country. Usually they were first world citizens with a cushy desk job who's biggest immediate concern was paying rent.

I fucking despised these people. Every time I hear them talking about how 'humans are a failed species' and 'the planet would be better off without us' I feel my blood boil. They sit on their high horses and declare moral judgment on all despite living in luxury that would have been unimaginable a century prior.

Credit where credit is due, I must thank them for helping me get over my cynicism. Never in my life have I felt more motivated to restore my faith in my county and humanity then when I met these snobby, misanthropic, entitled ass hats online.

It was around this point that I started becoming a transhumanist, in part as a reaction to that baseless cynicism but also as natural evolution of my interest in both science and engineering. I was already a big science nerd so the promise of the glorious transhumanist future didn't seem all that far fetched to me. As far as I am concerned there was no law of physics that prevented humans from transcending the limits of our mortal flesh, so why not do it?

It was at this point that I started reading science fiction books, mostly hard sci-fi stories but I also tried reading some of the more popular series that transhumanists often recommended. Which is where I started reading The Culture by Iain.M.Banks. (Don't ask me how I got access to those books in third world shithole, the answer is obvious.)

And Boy was it a ride.

A meaningless utopia

If you asked a random transhumanist these days "what would your ideal utopia looks like?" there is a good chance that they would point to the ASI run luxury communism civilization of the culture.

For those of you who never heard of the culture, it is a sci-fi series about a post-scarcity civilization run by benevolent god like ASIs known as the Minds. The stories usually focus on the lives of mortal sapient beings trying to find meaning in a post-scarcity society.

The first book in the series, Consider Phlebas was pretty good. It was a solid deconstruction of the 'macho action hero' tropes of its era and had some of the best world building I have ever seen from a sci-fi story.

But when I read the rest of the series a pattern emerged. The later books followed a pretty standard formula most of the time. The hero, often a member of the culture, usually a humanoid agent of Special Circumstances, is sent to a bleak dystopian civilization where they are guided by the culture minds to enact some needlessly complicated plot to put said civilization on track to a brighter future.

Most of the time the civilization dystopian nature is self inflected. Usually they are ruled over by corrupt elites or some such and they have to be over thrown for things to get better. In fact, almost all the misery in the culture universe is either self inflected or inflected by one civilization upon another. As far as I can remember there are no Dath ilans in the culture verse, no rational civilization that had not already reached post-scarcity status. Also a lot of the successful civilization have handed over control to either AIs or mind uploads.

The entire culture universe has this constant air of bleak pessimism to it. There is this running theme that civilizations just can't break free from the cycle of strife without the guiding hand of a technologically and morally superior civilization.

There is also the sense that the cultures Minds efforts to 'uplift' other civilizations aren't born out of their own altruism, but as an attempt to give their more miserable citizens, the ones who felt like their lives were meaningless, a reason to live. Like a twisted form of penance the Minds indulged in for robbing these people of a chance to make a difference, for their lives to mean something beyond simple pleasure.

Which seems to be the reason why sapient beings are hired by said Minds to act as agents in their overly elaborate plots, despite being able to complete those missions more effectively on their own and crucially, with fewer innocent lives lost.

Now I am well aware that this is for the most part just selection bias. The author can't exactly make a compelling story about a happy go lucky utopia with zero stakes. The stories of the culture aren't really representative of what the average civilization is really like because the author is obviously focusing on where the stakes are at, usually the barbaric civilization who are yet to break out of their self inflected dystopias.

But still it is quite telling that in the story State of the art, where a culture ship discovers Earth at the height of the cold war. One of the crew members suggest that our "incontestably neurotic and insane species" should be wiped out with a black hole.

I didn't really pay it much attention at the time because I never thought of the culture as a proper utopia. To me the culture was a prime example of meaningless utopia, where people play games of make believe, pretending that they are heroes making a difference in far off worlds while ignore the fact that they are usually nothing but a burden to their mission.

I refused to believe that anyone who truly understood the culture series actually thought that it was the kind of utopia we should strive for. Living as pets under the thumb of a machine god doesn't appeal to everyone and the story it self seems to acknowledge it. There are countless examples of culture citizens 'going native', renouncing their body enhancements and joining barbaric civilization to avoid the sense of meaninglessness that the culture exudes.

Unfortunate I was wrong. There are people out there who 'understood' the message and yet made it there life's mission to force this future on us, against our will and at the risk of extinction.

The faith of the faithless

Fast forward the early 2020s where I really started getting into rationalism. It was also the point at which I started to form my own views of the transhumanist community. From what I have gathered transhumanists seem to be split into two broad factions, I call them the optimists and the Singularitarians.

The optimist faction are generally focused on improving the human condition in the here and now. They have faith in humanity and believe that we can get our shit together and make a better world for our selves and our children. Examples of this are people who work on cryonics, anti-aging treatments and human intelligence augmentation. They are often young people with high agency who are not satisfied with the status quo but still believe that we can do better.

Then there are the Singularitarian faction, the ones who lost faith in humanity and believe that the only way forward is by building ASI. They are often the old guard of the transhumanist community, founders who once believed that the glorious transhumanist future would be built brick by brick by fellow humans. Yet now, perhaps out of a fear of their impending mortality or frustration at humanities constant failure to learn from their mistakes, many of them have became hardcore accelartionists who want the singularity to happen now, even if it meant everyone else would be forced to shoulder the risks with them.

I didn't take the second faction seriously until later on, partially because I refused to believe any sane person would actually think that building ASI before humanity gets their shit together was a remotely good idea. Often when I read the works of such people their world view sounded bleak and fundamentally anti-human. They seem to hold this pesudo-religious belief that humans are irreparably broken and that the only thing left for us to do is to summon a machine god and except what ever fate it decides for us. It was the same kind of sophisticated cynicism that I so visceral despised, just taken to a fanatic extreme.

At first these anti-human groups (not just in the transhumanist community but even in the broader world) were an annoying fringe minority, the kind you would ostracize and laugh out the room, but something happened between 2019 and now that either caused their numbers to swell or caused them to become much more vocal. The de-growth movement sweeping through Europe and the sudden push to ASI seem to be downstream of that.

Given the timelines it is easy to see a connection between this and recent global events. Our collective failure to contain covid or slowdown global warming, the war in Ukraine, the Isreal-Hamas war and the horrific atrocities committed during and after it, the rise of MAGA, the anti-vax movement and the return of the measles, the Epstein files and the US-Iran war. All of these are the kind of events that would make you question your faith in humanity.

Which brings me to the the core thesis of this essay. My hypothesis is that wide spread cynicism and apparent lose of faith in humanity is a major driving force behind the ASI race, important enough that if we remove it the race would grind to a halt. I would have to do some proper research before I can be sure of this but so far I think this hypothesis holds enough water to be worth testing.

But giving a proper empirical analysis of this hypothesis isn't the point of this essay. The point of this essay is to gesture broadly at this phenomenon so others can hopefully think about it, and also to ask a question of my fellow rationalist, the ones who still for some reason think current day humanity should build ASI.

If your faith in humanity was stronger then it is now, if you still had that unshakable belief that we would one day defeat the dragon tyrant and grasp the cosmic endowment, not with the hands of our creations but with our own hands.

Would you still want to build a machine god? Would you still roll that dice and risk extinction?

If so, what risk would you be willing to take? 1% chance of extinction? 10%? 0.1%? Do you think your fellow humans would be willing to take the risk with you? Why and why not?

Before you answer, I want you to entertain one last thought experiment.

A well earned utopia

The world of Dath ilan is a strange place. It is a median world where the median person in it resembles the author. In this case, the author is Eliezer Yudkowski. The world of Dath ilan is an alternate Earth with a single unified government where game theory and economics are taught in elementary schools, cryonics is a universal human right, most modern Earth problems like infectious disease and wars are basically not a thing and overall a much more coordinated and sane civilization. It is the kind of society that even the most paternalistic culture Mind would take one look at and decide that there is nothing to fix.

The most striking feature about Dath ilan is that unlike other utopias, it doesn't rely on speculative sci-fi technologies to justify its utopian society. Dath ilan is technologically in the same ballpark as Earth, they just used what technologies they have far more effectively then Earth ever did. While it wasn't really a utopian vision of Earth, it was still in a sense the ultimate expression of optimistic transhumanism, a utopia built brick by brick by humans for humans (and aliens if they ever decided to visit).

Now imagine this, imagine a version of Earth that was similar to Dath ilan, an Earth with free universal health care, free optional cryonic preservation for all, where all the money we burned on AI development could now be spent on putting an end to aging. An Earth with no wars, no genocide, no pay walled academic journals and no corrupt politicians. Basically the median world of the optimistic transhumanist.

Now take a random frontier lab employee and drop them into this hypothetical world. Do you think they would still endorse building ASI? What about An accelartionist from outside the labs? Would They still endorse their old world views in the face of this utopia?

What about you? Would you want to bring the technological singularity into that world?

I am willing to bet that more often then not, the answer to all these questions is no. Sure a more functional Earth would be better equipped to navigate the challenges of ASI alignment, yet at the same time they would have much less incentive to do so. There doesn't seem to be any near term extinction level natural disasters that a more coordinated humanity couldn't survive on their own, and our immediate cosmic neighborhood looks quite empty as well so grabby aliens don't seem to be an immediate issue either. With cryonics and anti-aging treatments mortality as a motivation is no longer a factor, so is world peace since wars in such a world would no longer be a thing.

So again I ask you dear reader, if you thought such utopia was achievable by you and your fellow humans, would you still want to build ASI?

I personally think it is possible. We often focus so much on the folly of a our species the we forget all the good things we have so far achieved. Diseases that were once a death sentence are now little more the a nuisance, child birth went from being a game of Russian roulette to a routine operation. We carved up mountains, split the atom, dove to the bottom of the oceans, flew above the sky and set foot on the moon.

Despite all the horrors, both the ones that I had seen first hand and the ones that read about in books, I still haven't lost faith in humanity, I still would refuse even a 1% chance of extinction in exchange for a 99% chance of utopia.

If we halt frontier AI development now and use even a tenth of the money we would have other wised spent on AI development, on actually solving real world problems like cryonics and life extension, I have no doubt in my mind that we would be able to bring about a truly well earned utopia. The kind of utopia that we can brag about to our children, the kind that would make them proud of us and make us proud of ourselves.

Not a meaningless hedonistic zoo, built through sheer blind luck in a fit of frantic hubris and ruled over by machine gods beyond our comprehension.

So I am asking you one last time, if you believed in your fellow humans, would you still risk it all on the singularity?

If you had faith in humanity, would you still pray to a machine god?



Discuss

item.title: Please just give me more time
item.description:
Last month we (my startup, Ovelle Bio) made a key breakthrough for our in vitro gametogenesis research. I can't describe it in too much detail, since we are still in the process of patenting it, but it resolves a longstanding challenge in the field, and I believe we have now found the paradigm that will solve IVG. We are on track to make full-grown human eggs from stem cells by mid-2028.

I believe that within 20 years (counting time for babies to reach adulthood) we will have human researchers who are much more capable than any who have ever lived to date.

For all those working in AI: all I need is some time. Please give me a chance.
